I have been asked to look at the staffing plan for the autumn peak at the Rugby site, and to say before the end of the month whether it will hold. I think the plan is sound in outline. The people who wrote it have run the building for years, and the numbers in it match the figures I was given by the finance team. The weak point is probably the packing team, which ran short in the second week of every peak on record. Perhaps that is bad luck, but three years in a row looks more like a pattern.

The agency team seems to arrive later than our own people, by maybe a quarter of an hour each shift. That sounds small. On a single day it is more or less harmless, since the morning queue at the benches takes some time to build in any case. Over a six-week peak, the lost minutes likely add up to several full shifts of packing. I suspect the agency is aware of this, since its staff tend to be booked early on the busiest days.

The plan assumes that each packer will manage the same rate in the evening as in the morning. That is arguably the most hopeful line in the whole document. At the sites I have worked with, the evening rate is apparently lower by a tenth or so, and at Rugby it is possibly lower still, because the evening shift has more new starters and fewer of the people who set up the benches. The planners presumably took the morning figure because it was the one to hand.

I guess the simplest fix is a small evening buffer, sort of a standing reserve of two packers who can move between benches as the queue shifts from one end of the row to the other. The cost would likely be modest. It is seemingly cheaper than the overtime we paid last year, when the evening shift ran two hours late on eleven nights in a row and the carriers charged us for every missed collection.

There is also a kind of habit at Rugby of moving people off packing whenever the goods-in team falls behind. I understand why. But that habit probably explains part of the shortfall in the second week, and nobody has written it down as a rule, so it is hard to see in the figures until you stand on the floor and watch it happen.

The returns bench is a smaller question, and maybe one for later. It is somewhat slower than last year, but the volume through it is lower too, and the two people who run it know their work and need no help from me.

Training is the last point. New starters learn the benches in three shifts, which is possibly quicker than the plan allows. If so, the induction day could be shortened, and the spare hours moved to the evening, where they would do the most good during the weeks that matter.

I will go through the rota with the site manager next week, and we will settle the evening buffer then. The rest of the plan can more or less stand as written. Perhaps the second week of this peak will look quite different from the last three.
